title: S-F-R
hookLine: sefer, sofer, sippur, mispar: book, scribe, story, number

lines: A RECEIPT IN A COAT POCKET.
cards: A crumpled receipt turns up in a coat pocket. A date, a time, a column of prices, a total. Read it again.
Candles, flour, a birthday card, at seven on a Thursday evening. Somebody was running late for a party. The numbers are telling a story.
English keeps counting and telling in separate drawers. Hebrew puts them in one root, and adds the book and the scribe. Samech, fey, resh: S-F-R.

teach.b: Turn S-F-R four ways. First, sefer, a book. A Torah scroll is a Sefer Torah, a book of Torah, though it's rolled, not bound.
Second, sofer, a scribe, the one who writes the book.
Yesterday's Ezra, whom you first met as a sofer on day eight hundred seventy-six, is called just that: "he was a ready scribe in the Law of Moses." Ready: quick, skilled.

teach.h: SIPPUR: TELL IN THE EARS OF THY SON.
teach.b: Third, sippur, a story, from the verb to tell. Before the last plagues in Egypt, Moses is told why these things are happening: "that thou mayest tell in the ears of thy son, and of thy son's son."
And the Psalms: "The heavens declare the glory of God." Declare is mesaprim, they tell. The night sky, telling a story with no words at all.
Fourth, mispar, a number, from the verb to count.

God brings Abram outside: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." And for the weeks between Passover and Shavuot, Leviticus says, "And ye shall count unto you," day by day.
The heavens tell, and Abram is asked to count them. A father tells his son, and a scribe writes it down. In Hebrew, counting and telling are cousins.
To count your days is to start telling their story, and a story told well counts what mattered.

how: A Sefer Torah is written by hand by a trained sofer, a scribe; at the Passover seder, families retell the Exodus, drawing on the command to tell it to one's children, and in the weeks after Passover Jews count the days of the Omer.

o: a root for counting and telling, and so books and scribes
a root for writing on stone, used for the commandments
a root for the shofar, the horn blown on the holidays

s: in Hebrew, to count and to tell come from the same root
mispar, number, and sippur, story, both come from S-F-R.
Psalm 19 says the heavens keep silent about God
"The heavens declare the glory of God": mesaprim, they tell.
a Torah scroll is not called a book because it's rolled
it's a Sefer Torah, a book of Torah, rolled or not.

games.q: God brings Abram outside under the night sky. what is he asked to do?
o: count the stars, if he can.
games.why: "count the stars, if thou be able to count them." then: so shall thy seed be.

practice: Count back a few days and stop on one small moment that stayed with you: something someone said, a meal, a wrong turn that went right.

Tell it to yourself start to finish, the way you'd tell it at a table, and find the detail that makes it yours. Then think of one person who'd like to hear it, and if you pray, hold the moment in the quiet.

wordCard.voice: S-F-R. Samech, fey, resh: sefer, a book; sofer, a scribe; sippur, a story; mispar, a number. Counting and telling in one root. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a book; from S-F-R, the root of counting and telling.

carryVoice: Your line: books, stories, numbers. The receipt in the coat pocket knew it all along. Rest well.
